name: Peanut
short: Allergy (1% to 4.5% of children): anaphylaxis, rarely fatal; peanut is a leading cause of fatal food anaphylaxis. Top inhaled item in 1 child series. Contaminated peanuts: aflatoxin, liver cancer.
text: Allergy is the main harm. A 2019 narrative review states that peanut allergy affects 1% to 4.5% of children, with the potential for severe reactions, persists in most people diagnosed with it, and that fatal anaphylaxis is rare. A 2026 meta-analysis states that peanut allergy affects 2% of children and 1% of adults. A 2010 review calls peanuts a frequent cause of food allergy and the most common cause of fatal food-induced anaphylaxis in the U.S., and a 2024 review reports peanuts and tree nuts as the leading causal foods of fatal food anaphylaxis in the United Kingdom and Canada. A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of 8 studies in children and adolescents with peanut allergy estimated 2.74 cases of anaphylaxis per 100 person-years and 12.28 accidental peanut exposures per 100 person-years. In a network that recorded 3,510 anaphylaxis cases from 2002 to 2020, 70 people (2%) had the most severe (grade 4) anaphylaxis and 25 of them died (19 food-related); the main allergens in these 70 severe cases were food (60%), with peanut given as 20% and milks as 11% (the abstract does not say whether these shares are of all 70 cases or of the food-related ones); three food-related severe cases, one fatal, occurred during oral food challenges in children. A 2018 review of 32 studies reports that young adults with asthma and a previously known food allergy, particularly to peanut or tree nuts, are at higher risk of fatal reactions, and that delayed adrenaline injection is associated with fatal outcomes. In people who already have peanut allergy, giving peanut by mouth as oral immunotherapy raises reactions: a 2019 meta-analysis of 12 randomized trials (1,041 participants, median age 8.7 years) found that it increased anaphylaxis (risk ratio 3.12), epinephrine use and serious adverse events compared with avoidance or placebo, and a 2020 meta-analysis of 27 studies (1,488 children) found that adverse events led 6.6% of children to stop and that 7.6% had reactions needing epinephrine; the 2026 meta-analysis of 20 randomized trials (2,161 participants, median age 8.6 years) also found a higher risk of anaphylaxis with oral immunotherapy (risk ratio 2.27). Choking risk in young children: in a 2020 study of 200 Chinese children with airway foreign bodies (92% under 3 years), peanuts were the most often inhaled item; 4 children needed chest surgery and 1 died during rigid bronchoscopy from acute respiratory failure (the abstract does not say what that child had inhaled). In a 2024 series of 171 children seen with suspected foreign-body inhalation (mean age at presentation 2.3 years), a foreign body was found in 83; 83% of the retrieved items were vegetable, of which peanut was the most common, and complications such as pneumothorax (collapsed lung) were seen in 2 cases. Contamination: a 2026 review states that aflatoxin B1, a fungal toxin that contaminates peanuts grown in warm regions, causes liver cancer, multiplies cancer risk together with chronic hepatitis B infection, and that peanuts are a major source of aflatoxin exposure in many populations; this is a harm of contaminated peanuts, not of peanut itself. The cited sources concern eating peanuts or peanut protein; none studied the peanut extracts tested in the 1960s. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
